summary: This informational document specifies ways to interconnect multiple TRILL sites across an MPLS network using existing TRILL and VPLS standards. It addresses connecting more than two sites and keeping TRILL transparent across the MPLS network.

plainLanguage.summary: Two playgrounds on different sides of a city can be joined by a hidden tunnel. This explains how to tunnel TRILL networks through an MPLS network.

questions: how to connect trill sites over mpls
subtitle: Connecting distant TRILL networks through a carrier's MPLS backbone.

tldr.problem: TRILL networks at different locations need to work together across MPLS carrier networks. The challenge is bridging them while maintaining transparency and supporting multiple sites.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two methods: a VPLS model that treats the MPLS network like an Ethernet bridge, and a VPTS model using virtual TRILL switches (VTSDs) and TRILL Intermediate Routers (TIRs) to create a unified emulated TRILL campus.
tldr.outcome: Organizations can now extend TRILL switching across geographically separated sites through MPLS networks without requiring TRILL awareness in the carrier's core routers.

today: RFC 8385 is an Informational RFC that describes these two methods for interconnecting TRILL sites across MPLS networks. It does not mandate implementation of either model but provides guidance for network designers choosing between them based on their infrastructure and requirements.

sections.title: Connecting TRILL Sites via MPLS
sections.content: TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links) is a protocol that provides optimal forwarding across multi-hop networks with support for multipath routing and loop prevention using hop counts. When TRILL sites are separated by an MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) network run by a service provider, direct TRILL forwarding is not possible. RFC 8385 solves two problems: connecting more than two TRILL sites across an MPLS provider network, and supporting multiple tenants (organizations) where each tenant has its own TRILL network isolated from others.
sections.plainLanguage: TRILL is like a smart office telephone system where calls find the best route automatically. MPLS is like a carrier network connecting far-away buildings. This explains how to make the smart telephone system work across the carrier network.

sections.title: Two Connection Models
sections.content:
The RFC presents two models. The VPLS Model (Virtual Private LAN Service) is simpler: it makes the MPLS network look like a single Ethernet broadcast domain. TRILL packets are forwarded transparently across MPLS pseudowires (which are virtual point-to-point links over the MPLS network) just as if they were traveling over Ethernet. TRILL adjacencies (neighbor relationships) are discovered automatically through IS-IS messages.

The VPTS Model (Virtual Private TRILL Service) is more sophisticated. Instead of treating MPLS as an Ethernet cable, TRILL Intermediate Routers (TIRs) at the edges of the MPLS network act like TRILL switches themselves. Virtual TRILL Switch Domains (VTSDs) inside each TIR form a single emulated TRILL campus across the MPLS cloud. Each VTSD maintains its own routing database and can support multiple tenants, segregating their traffic completely.
sections.plainLanguage: Model 1 is like treating the MPLS network as one giant Ethernet cable connecting distant offices. Model 2 is like having a TRILL switch at each office that talks to other TRILL switches across the MPLS network to create one unified smart switching system.

sections.title: VPLS Model Details
sections.content: In the VPLS model, TRILL Routing Bridges (RBridges) at each site connect to Provider Edge (PE) devices, which are standard VPLS routers. The PE devices do not need to understand TRILL; they simply forward Ethernet frames (which contain TRILL packets) over pseudowires to other PE devices. TRILL IS-IS control messages are transparently forwarded by the VPLS domain. Loop prevention relies on the split-horizon rule: a PE device does not forward traffic from one pseudowire to another within the same VPLS instance. No changes to standard VPLS implementations are required.
sections.plainLanguage: Picture the PE routers as postal workers who forward unopened envelopes (Ethernet frames) without caring what is inside. They never forward from one path back to where it came from, which prevents loops.

sections.title: VPTS Model and Tenants
sections.content: The VPTS model introduces new entities. A TRILL Intermediate Router (TIR) is a device that supports both MPLS and TRILL. Inside each TIR is at least one Virtual TRILL Switch Domain (VTSD), which acts like a TRILL RBridge. When multiple tenants are supported, each tenant gets its own VTSD, maintaining separate TRILL routing databases and traffic isolation. Each VTSD can have its own TRILL nickname (the identifier TRILL uses for routing). TIRs form pseudowire connections and appear to TRILL sites as if they are all connected to a single TRILL campus. The VPTS model does not use split-horizon; instead, TRILL's native loop prevention through distribution trees handles this.
sections.plainLanguage: A TIR is like a bilingual receptionist who speaks both the carrier language (MPLS) and the office language (TRILL). VTSDs inside the TIR are like separate reception desks for different customers, each with their own filing system and rules.

sections.title: Choosing a Model
sections.content: The VPLS model is simpler because it requires no TRILL logic at the carrier network edge; standard VPLS equipment suffices. The VPTS model requires TIR implementation but provides tighter integration as a unified TRILL campus and is the default for multi-tenancy. VPTS handles frame processing for multi-destination packets using TRILL's distribution trees and performs RPF (Reverse Path Forwarding) checks to prevent loops. The RFC notes that VPTS is preferred for interoperability because it emulates what TRILL expects when sites are truly part of one campus.
sections.plainLanguage: The VPLS model is like a courier service that just moves boxes without opening them. The VPTS model is like having a smart dispatch center that understands the contents and routes them optimally.
